}\\r\\n</style>\\r\\n</head>\\r\\n<body>\\r\\n<main>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h1>Role Question Answer Choices (The Hardest Thing about Role Questions)</h1>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>While the way in which we read the stimulus of any Role question is similar to how we approach Find the Conclusion questions, the answer choices we are faced with in Role questions are much more difficult. Life would be so simple if all the answer choices were just asking us if the statement in question is a premise or conclusion, but the test makers love to describe a relatively straightforward concept in abstract and vague language in Role question answer choices.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>As a result, the successful student should devote the majority of their time and energy to answer choices when approaching Role questions. As you get comfortable with analyzing the structure of the stimulus, it should become second nature to you. I use about 60% of all the time to examine answer choices in Role questions, with the other 40% set aside for reading the question and the stimulus.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>The ability to de-abstractify (translating vague and abstract terms that appear in answer choices into their stimulus equivalents) and knowing exactly what they are referring to is one of the most important skills that the advanced student needs to master. If you do not have this ability, often you will end up choosing a wrong answer choice even if you knew what you were looking for. You simply did not understand what the answer choice was trying to say. In other words, advanced students can read through a list of abstract answer choices and know exactly what they are referring to.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Take a look at the following answer choice examples, and see if you can decipher what is it that they are referring to, or even better, try to make up an argument with the components that would function as these answer choices describe:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<ol class=\\"choice-list\\">\\r\\n<li>It is used to illustrate the general principle that the argument presupposes</li>\\r\\n<li>It is an illustration of a premise that is used to support the argument’s conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It is used to counter a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It makes an observation that, according to the argument, is insufficient to justify the claim that the argument concludes is false</li>\\r\\n<li>It describes a phenomenon for which the argument’s conclusion is offered as an explanation</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a general principle whose validity the argument questions</li>\\r\\n<li>It denies a claim that the argument takes to be assumed in the reasoning it rejects</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a claim for which no justification is provided but that is required to establish the argument’s main conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a claim for which justification is provided and that, if true, establishes the truth of the argument’s main conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It is what the author’s argument purports to explain</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a hypothesis that the argument attempts to undermine by calling into question the sufficiency of the evidence</li>\\r\\n<li>It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole but is not the only explicitly stated conclusion in the argument</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a statement that the argument is intended to support but is not the conclusion of the argument as a whole</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a statement for which some evidence is provided and that itself is offered as support for the conclusion of the argument as a whole</li>\\r\\n<li>It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole and is supported by another statement for which support is offered</li>\\r\\n</ol>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Yep, that was brutal. You probably had no idea what many of these even meant. Not to worry, let’s break them down one by one:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>1. It is used to illustrate the general principle that the argument presupposes</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Whenever we are faced with an answer choice that looks super abstract, the first thing to do is to always <strong>extract what keywords we can</strong> to try to make sense of the whole thing. Three words stand out in this answer choice: “illustrate”, “general principle”, and “presuppose”.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Now certain words have specific meanings within the LSAT. All three of these words appear repeatedly in LR questions and we need to memorize them:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Presuppose:</strong> in daily usage, a presupposition can mean either an assumption or something that is necessary. On the LSAT presuppose simply means “require”. (It’s talking about a necessary condition, something that we will soon cover.)</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Illustrate:</strong> an illustration, as it appears in a LR question, is simply referring to an example/examples</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>General Principle:</strong> we briefly touched upon the nature of principles on the LSAT in the last chapter, and will do so again further down the road. But for now, just know that a principle is a rule on what we should/shouldn’t do; and that it applies to multiple conditions and scenarios.</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>For example, “<em>John is always tired in the morning, he should go to bed earlier</em>” is not a principle, we are just talking about one person here. “<em>Those who are tired in the morning should strive to get to bed earlier</em>” is a principle. It’s no longer just about John anymore, it is a recommendation for a certain category of people.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So now there are three requirements that must be met if we were to select this hypothetical answer choice as the correct answer. First, the statement in question must be an example; second, behind this example is a principle on what we should or shouldn’t do; and lastly, this principle is required in order for the author to advance their argument.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Take a look at this example:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">Despite a high paying job, John was extremely stressed out and depressed</span>, so there are intangible things in life that we must pursue to find true happiness.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John’s situation is the illustration of a general principle; namely that having a lot of money isn’t enough to make you happy. Is this principle required in order for the conclusion to stand? Yes, the conclusion says factors other than money must be considered in order to be happy. The underlined statement satisfies all three requirements and if this was a Role question, this would be the correct answer.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>2. It is an illustration of a premise that is used to support the argument’s conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Again, “<strong>Illustration</strong>” means example. So we know this answer choice is referring to an example in the stimulus. Furthermore, it is an illustration of a premise. So when examining this answer choice, we must isolate the premise/premises that appear in the argument and ask ourselves, is the quoted statement an example of what the premise is trying to say?</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>Here is an example to illustrate what this answer choice is trying to say:</strong></p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">John has been smoking two packs a day since he was sixteen, last week he was diagnosed with lung cancer.</span> Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer. We must avoid cigarettes at all costs if we want to stay healthy.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>What is the premise here?</strong> Smoking causes lung cancer. <strong>What is the conclusion?</strong> Don’t smoke. John’s case is an illustration of the causal relationship between smoking and lung cancer. Requirement satisfied.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>3. It is used to counter a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So right away, we should realize that “<em>a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</em>” is referring to a real or potential counter argument. A counter argument runs contrary to the author’s conclusion. If I say “going to college is a great way to enjoy a higher standard of living down the road,” but you respond with “but many college graduates have to take years to pay back debt”, you are making a counter argument in opposition to me.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Continuing with our example, if I had anticipated your potential objection/counter argument, I can say something along the lines of “college graduates enjoy higher income than their non college counterparts even with the cost of debt factored in.” What I’m doing, essentially, is anticipating your potential objection and shutting you down in advance. That’s what is meant by countering a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">College graduates make more money than they would if they didn’t go to college, even if they are paying off student loans plus interest.</span> So going to college is a great way to make more money and enjoy a better life.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Here, the underlined statement is both a premise as well as a pre-emptive strike against a potential objection, namely that graduates end up with so much debt that going to college doesn’t make sense.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>4. It makes an observation that, according to the argument, is insufficient to justify the claim that the argument concludes is false</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>A key piece of information we can extract from this answer choice is that there is a <em>claim that the argument concludes is false</em>. In other words, the author of this argument is arguing AGAINST a claim. Someone has made a claim, and the author is saying that claim is false.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So we have two viewpoints in this potential stimulus. The author’s argument is directed against an adversary.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Further, we know that the opponent made an observation in support of their view, but the author is saying that observation is not enough to prove anything, and subsequently goes on to argue that the opponent’s claim is false.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So in order for this answer choice to be correct, the stimulus must satisfy the following requirements: there must be an opposing view, the author must be arguing against this opposing view and declaring it false. The opponent must have provided an observation as a basis of support for their view, and the author must have made the claim that this observation is not enough to demonstrate the truth of the opponent’s view.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Let’s go a step further with a concrete example:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>John:</strong> <span class=\\"underlined\\">Celebrities have the biggest smiles in front of the camera</span>, so they must be the happiest people alive.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>David:</strong> That is not true. Many celebrities suffer from depression and substance abuse. Smiling in front of the camera doesn’t mean a thing, they could simply be putting on a show for the audience.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Does the underlined statement fit the requirement for this answer choice? Yes, David is arguing that John’s claim is false. David also suggests that the observation John makes in support of his claim is insufficient to justify his claim.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>5. It describes a phenomenon for which the argument’s conclusion is offered as an explanation</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Here is another key term that we must familiarize ourselves with: <strong>explanation</strong>.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Explanation: on the LSAT, the word “explanation” has a very strict and precise meaning, it simply means “cause.”</strong></div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So whenever you see the word “explanation” in an answer choice, check the stimulus for cause - effect reasoning. If it’s not there, then this answer would be wrong.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>What this answer choice is referring to is something we have seen before. We talked about questions where there is a cause and effect relationship in the argument, but instead of the cause being the premise and the effect being the conclusion, the order is reversed. The author describes a phenomenon and concludes what caused it. See PT43-S3-Q23 in the Find the Conclusion chapter if you had forgotten.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>We will reuse our example from the previous chapter:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">Smoking is a leading cause of lung cancer. <span class=\\"underlined\\">John has lung cancer</span>, therefore he must surely have been a heavy smoker.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John having lung cancer is the <strong>phenomenon</strong>, the author subsequently concludes that it must be smoking which caused his lung cancer. The cause - effect relationship goes like this: smoking → lung cancer, and the cause/explanation is in fact the conclusion in this example.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>6. It is a general principle whose validity the argument questions</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Again, this answer choice is referring to a general principle, but it’s a general principle that the argument is questioning/attacking. So if we are confronted with this answer choice, we must go back to the stimulus to make sure it satisfies two requirements: one, the quoted statement is indeed a general principle; and two, the author is arguing against the truth of this principle. Here is an example that would match what this answer choice is saying:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">It has been said that <span class=\\"underlined\\">the best way to approach any situation is to be yourself</span>. But this cannot be true. What if you are a selfish, egotistical or horrible person? Surely we must strive to better ourselves and be the best we can be?</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>7. It denies a claim that the argument takes to be assumed in the reasoning it rejects</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>This one is very similar to example 4. The argument is rejecting another person’s reasoning. So the author is arguing against someone else here. But are they rejecting that view outright? No, the author does something much more nuanced than that. The author thinks the reasoning used by their opponent has made an assumption, and instead of going after the opponent’s argument, our author is going after the opponent’s assumption.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So this answer choice is describing a stimulus in which there’s two arguments, the author’s argument and the opponent’s argument. This particular statement is the author rejecting an assumption made by the opponent’s argument.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>(We will look at the nature of assumptions in a subsequent chapter, as well as in Sufficient and Necessary Assumption question types.)</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>John:</strong> I’ve studied so hard for the finals, I’m definitely going to ace the exam!</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>David:</strong> <span class=\\"underlined\\">Studying hard doesn’t guarantee you will do well.</span> The exams are graded on a curve, and everyone else has studied just as hard.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>8. It is a claim for which no justification is provided but that is required to establish the argument’s main conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>There are two important pieces of information in this answer choice that can help us determine whether it’s the correct answer. First, it is “required” to establish the argument’s main conclusion. That means it’s necessary in order for the main conclusion to be valid. So there’s no way this answer choice is talking about the conclusion itself, it’s therefore either a premise or an intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Second, the answer choice says it’s a claim for which no justification is provided. Remember what we said about how to differentiate between premises and intermediate conclusions in the previous chapter? Premises support the conclusion but do not have any other statements supporting them, whereas intermediate conclusions both support the conclusion and are supported by premises. So when we have a statement which supports the conclusion but is not supported by others, it can only mean one thing: we are talking about a premise here.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So we are essentially talking about a premise that is required to establish the truth of the conclusion. In other words, if the premise was untrue, the conclusion would not stand. Take a look at the following example for more clarity:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">I found an Olympic gold medal in the swim team locker room. It must have originally belonged to John. John is always losing things and <span class=\\"underlined\\">he participated in the Olympics.</span></p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John’s participation in the Olympics is a requirement for the example’s conclusion to stand. In order for John to be the original owner of the medal, he MUST have been a participant at least.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John’s participation in the Olympics is also a premise that supports the example argument’s conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>9. It is a claim for which justification is provided and that, if true, establishes the truth of the argument’s main conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Very similar to the example listed above, but with two important caveats. This answer choice HAS justification provided, while supporting the main conclusion, so it’s an intermediate conclusion. It also <strong>guarantees/establishes</strong> the truth of the conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">All practicing lawyers must have passed the bar. John is a partner at a prestigious law firm and therefore <span class=\\"underlined\\">he is a practicing lawyer</span>, so he must have passed the bar.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John being a practicing lawyer is supported by the fact that he is a partner at a law firm. This satisfies the intermediate conclusion requirement. Does John being a practicing lawyer establish the fact that he has passed the bar? Yes, it is mentioned in the first statement/premise that all practicing lawyers must have passed the bar.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>10. It is what the author’s argument purports to explain</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>This is identical to example 5: the author describes an effect/result/phenomenon, and argues for a specific cause.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>11. It is a hypothesis that the argument attempts to undermine by calling into question the sufficiency of the evidence</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>What is a hypothesis?</strong> In science, a hypothesis is offered by scientists to try to explain a phenomenon in the physical world or universe. Why did different types of birds have physical features that are adapted to their physical environments? Darwin hypothesized that it is due to the fact that species can change over time, adapting to their environments via physical modifications generation after generation. Darwin came up with a hypothesis, which today we know as The Theory of Evolution, that has been supported by evidence gathered both by him and subsequent scientists. In other words, a hypothesis is simply a posited causal explanation of a phenomenon, explaining WHY something is the way it is.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>On the LSAT, the word “hypothesis” can be understood as a “potential explanation/potential causation”; it usually appears in science/medicine themed LR stimuli.</strong></div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So what is this answer choice saying? The argument is attempting to undermine this hypothesis. It does so by saying that the evidence out there is not enough to support such a hypothesis. So when we are going through answer choices and come to this, we must make sure that there is a hypothesis present in the stimulus (the quoted statement being that hypothesis), the author is challenging this hypothesis, and the author does so by suggesting that the available evidence is not enough to support this hypothesis.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>12. It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole but is not the only explicitly stated conclusion in the argument</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Two pieces of key information here. The first is straightforward: we are talking about the main conclusion here. But note that it “<em>is not the only explicitly stated conclusion in the argument</em>”. That can only mean one thing: we have an intermediate conclusion in the argument as well. So if confronted with this answer choice, make sure that one, the statement we are talking about is in fact the main conclusion of the argument; and two, the argument contains a separate intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>13. It is a statement that the argument is intended to support but is not the conclusion of the argument as a whole</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Something that is supported by the argument but is not the main conclusion, that’s an intermediate conclusion we are talking about here.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>14. It is a statement for which some evidence is provided and that itself is offered as support for the conclusion of the argument as a whole</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Same as above. The statement in question is supported by support, and supports the main conclusion. This is also the intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>15. It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole and is supported by another statement for which support is offered</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Same as example 12: the statement referred to by the answer choice is the main conclusion, and is supported by another statement for which support is offered. So the main conclusion is supported by an intermediate conclusion. When faced with an answer choice like this, make sure it is indeed the main conclusion that the question is asking us to analyze, and make sure the argument contains an intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"asterisk\\">***</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n</main>\\r\\n</body>\\r\\n</html>\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"f9910e","wall_time_seconds":0.8491497,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1780,"output":"            job the sentence does in the argument.\\r\\n          </p>\\r\\n        </div>\\r\\n      )}\\r\\n    </div>\\r\\n  );\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function WhyHardNote() {\\r\\n  return (\\r\\n    <div>\\r\\n      <Panel>\\r\\n        An abstract answer choice describes what part of an argument does, without naming what the argument is\\r\\n        about.\\r\\n      </Panel>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        Role, Method and Flaw questions are full of them. The stimulus talks about a pool, a library or a\\r\\n        dentist. The answer choices never do. They talk about \\"a premise,\\" \\"a claim,\\" \\"the conclusion.\\"\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n\\r\\n      <h3>See one</h3>\\r\\n      <WhichSentence />\\r\\n\\r\\n      <h3>Why they feel hard</h3>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        <strong>1. Everyday words, strict meanings.</strong> On the LSAT, \\"explanation\\" means cause and\\r\\n        \\"presuppose\\" means require. Read them the everyday way and you misread the choice.\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        <strong>2. Nothing to hold onto.</strong> There is no pool in the answer choice. You have to supply the\\r\\n        content yourself by going back to the stimulus.\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        <strong>3. One word can sink it.</strong> A choice can describe the argument perfectly except for one\\r\\n        word, like \\"proves\\" where the author only \\"suggests.\\" That one word makes it wrong.\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n\\r\\n      <h3>How this bootcamp fixes it</h3>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        First the words (Module 2). Then a routine for breaking any abstract choice into plain English (Module 3)\\r\\n        and matching every piece to the stimulus (Module 4). Then methods and traps (Modules 5 and 6). Module 7\\r\\n        puts it all together.\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n      <Panel tone=\\"yellow\\">An abstract choice is a description. Your job is to find what it describes.</Panel>\\r\\n\\r\\n      <h3>Answer Choice Traps</h3>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        For the hardest LR and RC questions, read each answer choice carefully. Look for suspicious keywords,\\r\\n        concepts and connections that seem out of place. These three types show why that habit matters.\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n\\r\\n      <h3>Type 1. Half right, half wrong</h3>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        A choice can be only partially correct. The first half may match, while the second half adds something\\r\\n        outside the scope of the argument. Read the whole answer word by word. One correct part doesn\'t make\\r\\n        the rest correct.\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n\\r\\n      <h3>Type 2. Describing something that did not happen</h3>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        Role, Method and Flaw answers describe a feature of the stimulus\'s argument. A choice that describes\\r\\n        something the author never does can be eliminated. Read it, think about what it means, isolate any\\r\\n        suspicious words and ask: <strong>does the author do this in the argument?</strong>\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n      <p>\\r\\n        Keep the question type in mind. Strengthen and Weaken answers can introduce information that isn\'t in\\r\\n        the stimulus. For those questions, being new information doesn\'t make an answer wrong.\\r\\n      </p>\\r\\n\\r\\n      <section className=\\"border-4 border-brutal-ink bg-brutal-yellow/30 p-5 md:p-6 my-8\\" aria-labelledby=\\"abstract-trap-type-three\\">\\r\\n        <h3 id=\\"abstract-trap-type-three\\" className=\\"mt-0\\">Type 3. Vague or abstract answer choices</h3>\\r\\n        <p>\\r\\n          The correct answer can be vaguely worded. That makes it harder to recognize what the choice is\\r\\n          referring to, but vagueness alone isn\'t a reason to eliminate it.\\r\\n        </p>\\r\\n        <p>\\r\\n          Extract the keywords and think about what they mean on the LSAT. A noun names a concept you need to\\r\\n          find in the stimulus. A verb names something the author needs to do. An adjective or adverb needs\\r\\n          to describe the argument\'s tone or strength correctly.\\r\\n        </p>\\r\\n        <p>\\r\\n          Then read the choice again and match what it describes to the stimulus\'s structure. Go back and\\r\\n          forth as often as you need. This skill gets easier with practice, but rushing past the keywords\\r\\n          gives you less practice at the very thing you need to learn.\\r\\n        </p>\\r\\n        <p>\\r\\n          Module 3 gives you the seven steps on their own page before the drill. You\'ll use them to slow\\r\\n          down, pull out the keywords and say what each choice means.\\r\\n        </p>\\r\\n        <p className=\\"mb-0 font-semibold\\">\\r\\n          Watch for an almost perfect answer with one word that makes it wrong, sitting beside a correct\\r\\n          answer that\'s more vaguely worded. Check the word against the stimulus. The more specific-sounding\\r\\n          answer doesn\'t win just because it\'s easier to picture.\\r\\n        </p>\\r\\n      </section>\\r\\n    </div>\\r\\n  );\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n// ---------------------------------------------------------------- Module 2\\r\\n\\r\\nconst STATEMENT_WORDS: { term: string; meaning: string; note?: string }[] = [\\r\\n  { term: \\"Premise\\", meaning: \\"A reason the author gives to support a conclusion.\\" },\\r\\n  { term: \\"Main conclusion\\", meaning: \\"The final point the author wants you to accept.\\" },\\r\\n  {\\r\\n    term: \\"Intermediate conclusion\\",\\r\\n    meaning: \\"A claim that gets support and then gives support to the main conclusion.\\",\\r\\n    note: \\"Also called a supported premise.\\",\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  { term: \\"Fact\\", meaning: \\"A statement about the world, taken as true.\\", note: \\"\\\\\\"Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.\\\\\\"\\" },\\r\\n  { term: \\"Decision\\", meaning: \\"A choice someone made or will make.\\", note: \\"\\\\\\"I\'m taking the train instead of the bus.\\\\\\"\\" },\\r\\n  {\\r\\n    term: \\"Principle (general principle)\\",\\r\\n    meaning: \\"A rule about what should or shouldn\'t be done that covers many cases.\\",\\r\\n    note: \\"\\\\\\"People who are tired every morning should go to bed earlier\\\\\\" is a principle. \\\\\\"John is tired every morning, so he should go to bed earlier\\\\\\" is not. It\'s about one person.\\",\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  {\\r\\n    term: \\"Generalization\\",\\r\\n    meaning: \\"A broad statement about what is.\\",\\r\\n    note: \\"\\\\\\"All swans are white.\\\\\\" A principle says what should be. A generalization says what is.\\",\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  {\\r\\n    term: \\"Hypothesis\\",\\r\\n    meaning: \\"A possible explanation: a proposed cause.\\",\\r\\n    note: \\"Not just any claim. A hypothesis is a guess about why something happened.\\",\\r\\n  },\\r\\n];\\r\\n\\r\\nconst ACTION_WORDS: { term: string; meaning: string; note?: string }[] = [\\r\\n  { term: \\"Illustrate\\", meaning: \\"Give an example.\\", note: \\"\\\\\\"It illustrates a principle\\\\\\" means it\'s an example of the principle.\\" },\\r\\n  {\\r\\n    term: \\"Presuppose\\",\\r\\n    meaning: \\"Require.\\",\\r\\n    note: \\"If the argument presupposes something, the argument falls apart without it.\\",\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  { term: \\"Explain\\", meaning: \\"Give the cause.\\", note: \\"Not add detail. An explanation is a cause.\\" },\\r\\n  { term: \\"Undermine\\", meaning: \\"Weaken. Push against.\\" },\\r\\n  {\\r\\n    term: \\"Defend\\",\\r\\n    meaning: \\"Argue that a position is right.\\",\\r\\n    note: \\"Saying why someone holds a view is not defending it.\\",\\r\\n  },\\r\\n];\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction WordGrid({ words, accent }: { words: typeof STATEMENT_WORDS; accent: \\"cyan\\" | \\"pink\\" }) {\\r\\n  return (\\r\\n    <div className=\\"grid md:grid-cols-2 gap-4 my-6\\">\\r\\n      {words.map((w) => (\\r\\n        <div key={w.term} className=\\"bg-white border-2 border-brutal-ink p-4 brutal-shadow-sm\\">\\r\\n          <div\\r\\n"}'}]

}, [index]);\n  const item = ANSWER_CHOICE_ITEMS[index];\n  const readyToReveal = Boolean(requirements.trim() && example.trim());\n\n  async function next() {\n    setBusy(true);\n    setSaveError(\"\");\n    const work = `What must be present:\\n${requirements.trim()}\\n\\nMy example argument and described statement:\\n${example.trim()}`;\n    const translated = await markTranslatorComplete(item.stemNumber, [], work);\n    const recorded = translated.ok && await markDrillComplete(item.id, \"translation\", false, undefined, undefined, \"source_exercise_ungraded\");\n    if (!translated.ok || !recorded || !recorded.ok) {\n      setSaveError(\"Your progress could not be saved. Identify the statement this answer choice describes.</label>\n      <textarea id=\"choice-example\" rows={6} maxLength={5000} value={example} disabled={busy || revealed} onChange={(event) => setExample(event.target.value)} className=\"w-full border-2 border-brutal-ink bg-white p-4 rounded\" />\n    </div>\n    {!revealed && <button onClick={() => { if (readyToReveal) setRevealed(true); }} disabled={!readyToReveal} className=\"brutal-btn bg-brutal-ink text-brutal-paper\">Show breakdown</button>}\n    {revealed && <>\n      <div className=\"bg-brutal-paper border-2 border-brutal-ink p-6\"><h2 className=\"text-2xl font-black mb-4\">The breakdown</h2><div data-testid=\"source-breakdown\" className=\"space-y-4 leading-relaxed [&_p]:my-4 [&_li]:my-2 [&_ul]:list-disc [&_ul]:pl-6 [&_.underlined]:underline [&_.example]:italic [&_.example]:border-l-4 [&_.example]:border-brutal-ink [&_.example]:pl-4 [&_.definition]:my-4 [&_.definition]:border [&_.definition]:border-brutal-ink [&_.definition]:bg-brutal-yellow/20 [&_.definition]:p-4\" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: item.breakdownHtml }} /></div>\n      <p className=\"text-sm leading-relaxed\">Compare your work with the breakdown. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 14.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"7b529f","wall_time_seconds":0.4686371,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":503,"output":"681:export const ROLE_CHOICE_INTRO_HTML = \\"<p>While the way in which we read the stimulus of any Role question is similar to how we approach Find the Conclusion questions, the answer choices we are faced with in Role questions are much more difficult. Life would be so simple if all the answer choices were just asking us if the statement in question is a premise or conclusion, but the test makers love to describe a relatively straightforward concept in abstract and vague language in Role question answer choices.</p>\\\\n\\\\n<p>As a result, the successful student should devote the majority of their time and energy to answer choices when approaching Role questions. As you get comfortable with analyzing the structure of the stimulus, it should become second nature to you. I use about 60% of all the time to examine answer choices in Role questions, with the other 40% set aside for reading the question and the stimulus.</p>\\\\n\\\\n<p>The ability to de-abstractify (translating vague and abstract terms that appear in answer choices into their stimulus equivalents) and knowing exactly what they are referring to is one of the most important skills that the advanced student needs to master. If you do not have this ability, often you will end up choosing a wrong answer choice even if you knew what you were looking for. You simply did not understand what the answer choice was trying to say. In other words, advanced students can read through a list of abstract answer choices and know exactly what they are referring to.</p>\\\\n\\\\n<p>Take a look at the following answer choice examples, and see if you can decipher what is it that they are referring to, or even better, try to make up an argument with the components that would function as these answer choices describe:</p>\\";\\r\\n682:export const ROLE_CHOICE_SOURCE_SHA256 = \\"c914b12b0d61ba8e743e5e55979e48772d3147edcbc2b3dc305648fb3492ba61\\";\\r\\n685:export const ROLE_CHOICE_SOURCE_CONTENT_SHA256 = \\"c914b12b0d61ba8e743e5e55979e48772d3147edcbc2b3dc305648fb3492ba61\\";\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"73e3fb","wall_time_seconds":0.6603702,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":240,"output":"\\r\\nexport function useAuth() {\\r\\n  const context = useContext(AuthContext);\\r\\n  if (!context) {\\r\\n    // Defensive fallback — can occur during HMR / fast-refresh when the\\r\\n    // provider module is briefly out of sync with consumers. text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"Add-Content -LiteralPath 'C:\\Users\\Joshu\\dev\\ai-os\\brainstorms\\2026-10-13-abstract-answer-choice-drill.md' -Value @'\n\n### Separate review progress, saved drafts and contrapositive reading benchmark, 2026-10-13\n\nJoshua requested a full 15-choice run with retained progress, plus stronger instruction hierarchy using the existing contrapositive note as the visual standard. The implementation now keeps reviewed breakdowns separate from completed written exercises. Reveal records an actual rendered source breakdown as source_breakdown_reviewed; written requirements/example work uses source_exercise_ungraded. Both tags are ungraded and excluded from accuracy, trap/confidence statistics and mastery. Reviewing cannot replace or erase written evidence, and the end screen says how many breakdowns were reviewed and how many written exercises were saved instead of generic module completion.\n\nA validated, source-fingerprint-versioned session stores current choice, revealed state, reviewed/practiced IDs and per-choice unfinished text. Preview and each account have separate keys. Typing is saved immediately; browser progress and drafts survive navigation/reload. Existing cloudMirror provides draft mirroring, and existing drill-attempt APIs store signed-in review/written history without a schema migration. Account-owner hydration gates, per-await owner guards and confirmed-success source attempts prevent old-account state or failed optimistic saves from becoming another account's progress. Delayed cloud restoration does not overwrite an active draft. Storage/account failures are surfaced; reviewed drafts remain editable for continuing written work.\n\nThe visual benchmark was inspected in the current checkout: ContrapositiveNote in src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/OpeningCourseContent.tsx with opening.css, opening-course.css and contrapositive-visuals.css. Its reading hierarchy was adapted into the source exercise: 19px desktop body with 1.8 line height, regular Georgia section headings, navy definition panels, selective bold and distinct requirement/example colors. No conditional examples, media or teaching were imported. The exact source choice/breakdown HTML and order remain unchanged. The completion report now separates reviewed breakdowns from written work and does not describe ungraded reviews as incorrect graded drills.\n\nFinal focused checks passed: 24 tests across six files, including all 15 review-only items, finished-summary remount, unfinished drafts/current reveal, separate written saves, account switching during hydration and pending writes, failed-review retry, source fidelity and navigation regression. Typecheck, production build (including prebuild/postbuild verification) and diff check all passed. Root's local browser run verified reviewed counts 1 through 15 with written count 0, a 15-reviewed/0-written summary that survived reload/reopen, partial item-1 draft and revealed-state restoration, then item-1 written practice yielding 15-reviewed/1-written with item-2 cursor/count retained after reload. Desktop/docked instruction emphasis was clear; actual 300px and 375px viewports had no horizontal overflow. Root left the preview at item 2.\n\nThis is local preview acceptance only. '{"chunk_id":"206fd6","wall_time_seconds":0.4065676,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1401,"output":"      <figure className=\\"my-8 rounded-lg border-2 border-brutal-ink bg-brutal-paper p-5 md:p-7\\" aria-label=\\"John’s case illustrates the premise, which supports the conclusion\\">\\r\\n        <div className=\\"rounded-lg border-2 border-brutal-ink bg-brutal-yellow/30 p-4 md:p-5\\">\\r\\n          <p className=\\"mb-2 text-sm font-bold uppercase tracking-wider\\">The example</p>\\r\\n          <p className=\\"underline decoration-2 underline-offset-4\\">John has been smoking two packs a day since he was sixteen, last week he was diagnosed with lung cancer.</p>\\r\\n        </div>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"flex flex-col items-center py-3 font-bold text-brutal-ink\\">\\r\\n          <span>illustrates</span><ArrowDown className=\\"mt-1 h-6 w-6\\" aria-hidden=\\"true\\" />\\r\\n        </div>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"rounded-lg border-2 border-brutal-ink bg-brutal-paper p-4 md:p-5\\">\\r\\n          <p className=\\"mb-2 text-sm font-bold uppercase tracking-wider\\">The premise</p>\\r\\n          <p className=\\"font-semibold\\">Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer.</p>\\r\\n        </div>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"flex flex-col items-center py-3 font-bold text-brutal-ink\\">\\r\\n          <span>supports</span><ArrowDown className=\\"mt-1 h-6 w-6\\" aria-hidden=\\"true\\" />\\r\\n        </div>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"rounded-lg border-2 border-brutal-ink bg-brutal-yellow/30 p-4 md:p-5\\">\\r\\n          <p className=\\"mb-2 text-sm font-bold uppercase tracking-wider\\">The conclusion</p>\\r\\n          <p className=\\"font-semibold\\">We must avoid cigarettes at all costs if we want to stay healthy.</p>\\r\\n        </div>\\r\\n      </figure>\\r\\n\\r\\n      <p>If we only noticed that the paragraph discusses smoking, we would miss the structure. If we only noticed that John’s case is an example, we would leave part of the choice unchecked. We need to know what it is an example of and how that idea is used in the argument.</p>\\r\\n      <p>This explains the source example’s role. It does not ask us to decide whether the argument has proved its causal claim. The task here is to understand the description and identify the relationship the source is showing.</p>\\r\\n    </section>\\r\\n  );\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function RoleChoicePracticeInstructions() {\\r\\n  return (\\r\\n    <section className={PROSE} aria-labelledby=\\"role-choice-concrete\\">\\r\\n      <h2 id=\\"role-choice-concrete\\" className={HEADING}>Make each choice concrete</h2>\\r\\n      <p>For each of the fifteen choices, there are two pieces of written work you can use to test your understanding.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"space-y-5 rounded-lg border-2 border-brutal-ink bg-brutal-paper p-5 md:p-6\\">\\r\\n        <p><strong>State the requirements.</strong> What would have to appear in an argument for the choice to describe it correctly? Keep every part of the description. A claim receiving support is different from a claim receiving no justification. A claim being required is different from a claim establishing the conclusion.</p>\\r\\n        <p><strong>Create an example argument.</strong> Write reasons and a conclusion, then identify the particular statement the choice would describe. Check where each requirement appears in your example. If one part is missing, you know what still needs work.</p>\\r\\n      </div>\\r\\n      <p>The original breakdown is available whenever you need it. You can try the written work first, open the explanation to learn the relationship, or return to revise your example after reading. Reading the breakdown and completing the written work are recorded separately.</p>\\r\\n      <p>As you continue, keep comparing the wording of the choice with what the statement actually does. The explanation should make the language more concrete. Your example gives you a chance to use that meaning yourself.</p>\\r\\n    </section>\\r\\n  );\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function RoleChoiceClosing() {\\r\\n  return (\\r\\n    <section className={PROSE} aria-labelledby=\\"role-choice-whole-description\\">\\r\\n      <h2 id=\\"role-choice-whole-description\\" className={HEADING}>Check the whole description</h2>\\r\\n      <p>The fifteen choices use different words, but the task stays the same: turn the description into requirements you can check.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Start with the idea the choice names. Is it an example, a principle, an observation, a hypothesis, or a conclusion? Then look at what happens to that idea. Is it used as support, challenged, denied, or offered as an explanation?</p>\\r\\n      <p>Keep the strength of the wording. <strong>Required</strong> and <strong>establishes</strong> do different work. <strong>Attempts</strong> does not tell us that the attempt succeeds. <strong>Explicitly stated</strong> asks for something the argument actually says. Leaving out one of these details changes the description you are trying to satisfy.</p>\\r\\n      <p>The final choices also show why we trace each link of support. A statement can receive support and then support the main conclusion. Or it can be the main conclusion, supported by another statement that itself receives support. Ask why we should believe each claim and look for the reason the argument gives. Then ask what that claim supports in turn.</p>\\r\\n      <p>You can return to any choice and check your own example against its original breakdown. Have you included every required part? Have you identified the statement the choice describes? Does that statement actually do what the full choice says?</p>\\r\\n      <p className=\\"rounded-lg border-2 border-brutal-ink bg-brutal-yellow/30 p-5 md:p-6 font-semibold\\">That completes this lecture. When you later meet this language in a full LSAT question, look for those same parts and relationships in the argument you are given.</p>\\r\\n    </section>\\r\\n  );\\r\\n}\\r\\n"}'}]

Its snapshot is dated 2026-08-03; this is source evidence, not a current live-backend check.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Module 4 draft: match every requirement to the argument\\r\\n\\r\\nPurpose: move from describing what an answer needs to pointing to the actual parts of one full source argument. Unlike Module 3’s learner-created examples, this lesson supplies the argument and asks the learner to locate the relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### A description has to fit this argument\\r\\n\\r\\nAn answer choice can sound familiar and still describe the wrong relationship. Now we’ll use an argument that is already written. For every requirement in the choice, we need to point to the part of that argument that fulfills it.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead this original exchange:\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>John:</strong> <span class=\\"underlined\\">Celebrities have the biggest smiles in front of the camera</span>, so they must be the happiest people alive.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>David:</strong> That is not true. Many celebrities suffer from depression and substance abuse. Smiling in front of the camera doesn’t mean a thing, they could simply be putting on a show for the audience.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\nThe statement we are examining is John’s observation that celebrities have the biggest smiles in front of the camera. David is responding to John’s argument. Keep those two speakers separate as we read the choice.\\r\\n\\r\\nHere is the original answer choice:\\r\\n\\r\\n> It makes an observation that, according to the argument, is insufficient to justify the claim that the argument concludes is false\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Find the claim the author rejects\\r\\n\\r\\nThe choice says that the argument concludes a claim is false. Which claim?\\r\\n\\r\\nJohn says celebrities must be the happiest people alive. David opens with “That is not true,” then points to depression and substance abuse. So the rejected claim is John’s conclusion about their happiness. The statement under examination is not David’s objection. It is the observation John used to reach the claim David rejects.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Find the observation and check whether it is enough\\r\\n\\r\\nJohn’s reason is the smiles he sees in front of the camera. David says smiling “doesn’t mean a thing” and suggests celebrities could be putting on a show. David is challenging what those smiles establish. They do not justify John’s conclusion, according to David’s argument.\\r\\n\\r\\nWe can now match the description completely:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Requirement in the choice | Where it appears in the original argument |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| An observation is made | John: celebrities have the biggest smiles in front of the camera |\\r\\n| The observation is used to justify a claim | John uses the smiles to conclude celebrities are the happiest people alive |\\r\\n| The author treats the observation as insufficient | David says the smiles do not establish happiness and could be a performance |\\r\\n| The argument concludes the supported claim is false | David rejects John’s claim and cites depression and substance abuse |\\r\\n\\r\\n**False describes the claim David rejects. It does not describe the observation about the smiles.** That difference matters. If we moved “false” onto the observation, we would be reading a different choice.\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore accepting a description, say which statement it refers to and point to every relationship it requires. A passage containing all the right topics is not enough. The right statements must be doing the right jobs.\\r\\n\\r\\nPractice instruction draft: reread the original exchange and choice. Identify the observation, the claim it supports, and David’s response in separate written lines. Compare each line with the matching table. This is a source comparison, not an invented multiple-choice question.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Module 5 draft: see the actual move, not just the topic\\r\\n\\r\\nPurpose: identify how the author uses a reason to challenge a conclusion. This adds an actual worked method question, rather than a methods-label list.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Follow the rule to the case the economist chooses\\r\\n\\r\\nThe argument below is about taxation. That is its subject. The question asks how the economist responds to the politician, so we need to follow what the economist does with the politician’s reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Original question PT103-S1-Q18**\\r\\n\\r\\nPolitician: A government that taxes incomes at a rate of 100 percent will generate no revenue because all economic activity will cease. So it follows that the lower the rate of income tax, the more revenue the government will generate by that tax.\\r\\n\\r\\nEconomist: Your conclusion cannot be correct, since it would mean that an income tax of 0 percent would generate the maximum revenue.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Original question stem:** Which one of the following argumentative strategies is used by the economist in responding to the politician?\\r\\n\\r\\n**A.** stating a general principle that is incompatible with the conclusion the politician derives\\r\\n\\r\\n**B.** providing evidence that where the politician’s advice has been adopted, the results have been disappointing\\r\\n\\r\\n**C.** arguing that the principle derived by the politician, if applied in the limiting case, leads to an absurdly false conclusion\\r\\n\\r\\n**D.** undermining the credibility of the politician by openly questioning the politician’s understanding of economics\\r\\n\\r\\n**E.** attacking the politician’s argument by giving reason to doubt the truth of a premise\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nStart with the politician’s conclusion: the lower the income-tax rate, the more revenue the tax generates. The politician takes the result at a 100-percent rate and draws a broad relationship between lower rates and higher revenue.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe economist does not cite a country where a tax cut failed. She does not dispute that economic activity would cease at the 100-percent rate. She takes the politician’s conclusion to the other end of the range: a rate of zero percent.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf lowering the rate always raises revenue, a zero-percent rate would produce the maximum. But a tax charged at zero percent collects no income-tax revenue. The economist uses that consequence to challenge the politician’s conclusion.\\r\\n\\r\\n**That is the reasoning move: apply the politician’s rule at its lower limit and show that the resulting conclusion cannot be right.**\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Connect that move to the answer’s language\\r\\n\\r\\nChoice C calls the politician’s conclusion a **principle**. Here it is the general relationship the politician claims: lower rate, more revenue. **If applied in the limiting case** refers to applying that relationship at the zero-percent rate. **Leads to an absurdly false conclusion** refers to the claim that a zero-percent income tax would generate maximum revenue.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach part names something we can point to. The answer is C in the captured source key.\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice how other choices change the action. B describes real results from places that adopted the advice; no such evidence is given. D describes an open attack on the politician’s understanding of economics; the economist instead points to a consequence of the politician’s conclusion. E says a premise is challenged; the response challenges the conclusion drawn from the premise.\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore selecting a methods label, explain the actual move in ordinary words. Here, “the economist uses a zero-percent tax to show what goes wrong with the politician’s rule” connects the reason to the response. “They disagree about taxes” does not.\\r\\n\\r\\nPractice draft: identify the politician’s rule, the case the economist applies it to, and the result that makes the rule untenable. Then match those three parts to C. This is a worked source question; no new seventeen-category bank is added.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Module 6 draft: a possible explanation is not a proven explanation\\r\\n\\r\\nPurpose: diagnose the precise word or relationship that makes a close description go beyond the argument.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Keep the author’s degree of commitment\\r\\n\\r\\nA description can correctly identify the topic and still say the author did more than the passage shows. Read this full original question. Pay attention to **unwarranted**, **might instead**, and **might then** in the stimulus.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Original question PT139-S1-Q23**\\r\\n\\r\\nAnthropologist: Every human culture has taboos against eating certain animals. Some researchers have argued that such taboos originated solely for practical reasons, pointing out, for example, that in many cultures it is taboo to eat domestic animals that provide labor and that are therefore worth more alive than dead. But that conclusion is unwarranted; taboos against eating certain animals might instead have arisen for symbolic, ritualistic reasons, and the presence of the taboos might then have led people to find other uses for those animals.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Original question stem:** In the argument, the anthropologist\\r\\n\\r\\n**A.** calls an explanation of a phenomenon into question by pointing out that observations cited as evidence supporting it are also compatible with an alternative explanation of the phenomenon\\r\\n\\r\\n**B.** establishes that an explanation of a phenomenon is false by demonstrating that the evidence that had been cited in support of that explanation was inadequate\\r\\n\\r\\n**C.** rejects the reasoning used to justify a hypothesis about the origins of a phenomenon, on the grounds that there exists another, more plausible hypothesis about the origins of that phenomenon\\r\\n\\r\\n**D.** argues in support of one explanation of a phenomenon by citing evidence incompatible with a rival explanation\\r\\n\\r\\n**E.** describes a hypothesis about the sequence of events involved in the origins of a phenomenon, and then argues that those events occurred in a different sequence\\r\\n"}'}]
